inlines.text: 《华尔街日报》的一篇报道暗示，黄仁勋被排挤出局，更多是因为他的商业操作，而不是他的私生活。

blocks.text: 据《华尔街日报》报道，黄仁勋在任期间，英伟达推出了一项高风险的信贷计划。公司向AI云服务商和数据中心开发商提供数十亿美元的财务担保，让它们买得起英伟达芯片。黄仁勋的女婿尼科·卡普雷兹（Nico Caprez）力推这项计划，并向合作伙伴承诺快速成交。作为回报，云服务商要把一部分收入分给英伟达。

blocks.text: “像一只被车灯照住的鹿”

inlines.text: “像一只被车灯照住的鹿”

blocks.text: 最大的一笔交易是与OpenAI谈判，为俄亥俄州的一个数据中心提供2500亿美元担保。交易公开后，英伟达股价下跌5%。随后，此前担任CFO的临时CEO科莱特·克雷斯（Colette Kress）把英伟达对OpenAI的承诺砍掉了一半。缩减后的协议于8月签署。

blocks.text: 据《华尔街日报》报道，克雷斯此前已在内部质疑这些担保如何估值、能带来什么回报，并试图约束卡普雷兹。据称在8月的一次会议上，黄仁勋称她“像一只被车灯照住的鹿”，还贬低她只是个“负责汇报的CFO”，在战略和决策上帮不上他。至少从去年起，英伟达及其他云和芯片公司的循环AI交易就因吹大泡沫而受到批评。

blocks.text: 在10月柏林GTC大会上，黄仁勋借一个日本汤店老板的故事向六位云服务商CEO施压。他说自己排了很长的队，喝到了人生中最好喝的汤之一。当他想要第二碗时，老板拒绝了，因为排队的人太多，汤也快卖完了。据《华尔街日报》报道，黄仁勋对CEO们说：“他比你们所有人都更懂做生意。”

blocks.text: 这个故事的道理是，汤店老板没有把全部库存卖给一两个顾客。他保持高价，同时让客源保持广泛。黄仁勋说，云服务商没有照这个例子做，而是把过多算力卖给少数几个大客户，没有分散到众多买家手中。“你们没有在建立我产品的价值，”黄仁勋说。

blocks.text: A WSJ report suggests Jensen Huang was pushed out more over his business practices than over his affairs.

inlines.text: A WSJ report suggests Jensen Huang was pushed out more over his business practices than over his affairs.

blocks.text: Nvidia built a risky credit program under Huang, the Wall Street Journal reports. The company offered AI cloud providers and data center developers billions of dollars in financial guarantees so they could afford Nvidia chips. Huang's son-in-law Nico Caprez pushed the program and promised partners quick closings. In return, the cloud providers were supposed to give Nvidia a cut of their revenue.

inlines.text: Nvidia built a risky credit program under Huang, the
Wall Street Journal

reports. The company offered AI cloud providers and data center developers billions of dollars in financial guarantees so they could afford Nvidia chips. Huang's son-in-law Nico Caprez pushed the program and promised partners quick closings. In return, the cloud providers were supposed to give Nvidia a cut of their revenue.

blocks.text: "A deer in the headlights"

inlines.text: "A deer in the headlights"

blocks.text: The largest deal involved talks with OpenAI over a $250 billion guarantee for a data center in Ohio. Nvidia shares fell 5% after the deal became public. Interim CEO Colette Kress, who had been CFO, then cut Nvidia's commitment to OpenAI in half. The scaled-back deal was signed in August.

inlines.text: The largest deal involved talks with OpenAI over a $250 billion guarantee for a data center in Ohio. Nvidia shares fell 5% after the deal became public. Interim CEO Colette Kress, who had been CFO, then
cut Nvidia's commitment to OpenAI in half
. The scaled-back deal was signed in August.

blocks.text: According to the WSJ, Kress had already questioned internally how the guarantees were valued and what they would return and had tried to rein in Caprez. In an August meeting, Huang reportedly called her "a deer in the headlights" and dismissed her as a mere "reporting CFO" who didn't help him with strategy or decision-making. Circular AI deals by Nvidia and other cloud and chip companies have drawn criticism since at least last year for inflating a bubble.

blocks.text: Nvidia's stock valuation also reportedly frustrated Huang. The company's average monthly stock multiple fell from 23 to 16 between May and October, and Nvidia responded with the largest share buyback in its history.

blocks.text: Huang apparently feared he had made a losing bet

blocks.text: Major cloud providers were planning to adopt alternative chips and reduce their dependence on Nvidia. With Nvidia committed to buying large volumes of wafers and memory, Huang described the threat as an “avalanche” rolling toward the chipmaker.

blocks.text: At the GTC conference in Berlin in October, Huang used a story about a soup vendor in Japan to put pressure on half a dozen cloud CEOs. He said he had stood in a long line and eaten one of the best soups of his life. When he asked for seconds, the vendor said no because too many people were waiting and he was running out of soup. "He's a better businessperson than all of you," Huang told the CEOs, according to the WSJ.

inlines.text: At the GTC conference in Berlin in October, Huang used a story about a soup vendor in Japan to put pressure on half a dozen cloud CEOs. He said he had stood in a long line and eaten one of the best soups of his life. When he asked for seconds, the vendor said no because too many people were waiting and he was running out of soup. "He's a better businessperson than all of you," Huang told the CEOs, according to the WSJ.

blocks.text: The reasoning behind the story was that the soup vendor didn't sell his whole inventory to one or two customers. He kept prices high and his customer base broad. Huang said the cloud providers weren't following that example and were selling too much compute to a handful of big customers instead of spreading it across many buyers. "You are not establishing the value of my products," Huang said.
